title: Engaged Buddhism
hook: practice put to work for peace, justice and the earth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Secular Buddhism: people who keep the practice and set rebirth aside, and others who disagree. Your line was each explains itself. Did you hear one view out in its own words? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

Bombs are falling near a village. In the temple, the monks and nuns face a question no rulebook settles for them. Do we stay in the meditation hall and keep our practice, or do we go out and help the wounded? A Vietnamese Zen teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, told this story for years afterward, and the answer he gave was neither one. Both. Go out and help, and keep the practice while you do it. Breathe while you carry the stretcher. That answer has a name now. Today: Engaged Buddhism.

First, the name. The phrase engaged Buddhism is closely tied to Thich Nhat Hanh and the war years in Vietnam. It means practice that does not stop at the door of the meditation hall. The same attention you bring to a breath, you bring to a hungry neighbor, a broken law, a cut-down forest. Second, the old root. Engaged Buddhists do not say they invented anything. They point back to the Buddha's own teaching on compassion, karuna, the wish that someone's suffering would end. And they point to lines like this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule, the text says. Engaged Buddhists take it into protests, peace talks and courtrooms. Third, the many forms. In Sri Lanka, a village movement called Sarvodaya brings neighbors together to build roads and dig wells, and treats the shared work as practice. In Thailand, some monks have wrapped orange robes around old trees, ordaining them, so that cutting them down feels like harming a monk. Elsewhere, engaged Buddhists work on prisons, poverty and the climate. Fourth, the warning inside it. Engaged teachers say that anger dressed up as justice burns people out, and that a calm mind is part of the work, not a break from it. And not every Buddhist teacher puts the weight in the same place. Some say inner work comes first and action flows from it. Others say the two can't be pulled apart. Each explains itself. What engaged Buddhists share is the picture from the village: the stretcher in your hands, the breath in your chest, both at once.
screen: `PRACTICE OUTSIDE THE HALL.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `ROADS, WELLS, ORDAINED TREES.` · `A CALM MIND IS PART OF THE WORK.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN ACTION.`

segments.voice: Here is a way to try it, if you'd like. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Now bring to mind one small thing in your world that needs a hand: a neighbor who is struggling, a street with litter on it, a cause you have been meaning to look up. Don't solve it yet. Just breathe with it for a few breaths, the way the monks breathed with the stretcher. Then choose one act you could do today, small enough to really do. Hold that act in mind, and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Engaged Buddhism. Buddhist practice put to work in the world, for peace, justice and the earth, with the calm of the meditation hall carried into it. Today's word.
Your line: practice in action. Today, do the one engaged act you chose, and try to keep a single calm breath going while you do it. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Engaged Buddhists bring meditation and the teaching on compassion into social work, peace work, village development and care for the earth, often treating the work itself as practice.

what it means: practice that carries the calm of the meditation hall into helping, healing and protecting.
what a scholar hears: a name tied to Thich Nhat Hanh and wartime Vietnam, rooted by its teachers in karuna and in the Dhammapada's old rule.
